To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the use of DRM technology in digital distribution systems can compromise users’ privacy, and that this can be done intentionally by the system designers; (2) privacy engineering principles can mitigate the loss of privacy, but they cannot eliminate it; and (3) the most effective privacy engineering principle is “don’t collect data you don’t need.”
DRM systems can be designed to protect users’ privacy and that the security R&D and privacy R&D communities need to work more closely together to design such systems.
DRM can be a privacy problem but that it can also be a privacy solution.

the privacy problems that arise in the context of DRM and with how DRM systems should be designed to address those problems.
the privacy implications of DRM, and we argue that the privacy problems raised are serious enough to require the attention of the privacy R&D community.

privacy engineering for DRM is an open field, and that it is important for the security R&D and privacy engineering communities to pay attention to this field.
